strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important audio restoration problem, and the idea of performing inpainting in a discrete audio-token space is plausible and timely given recent audio codec and discrete diffusion work.

The method combines reasonable components: WavTokenizer for compact discrete representations, a transformer-based discrete diffusion model, and waveform-level replacement with crossfading to reduce boundary artifacts.
The evaluation uses several complementary objective metrics, including FAD, LSD, and ODG, and compares against classical and diffusion-based baselines from prior work across multiple gap lengths.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is insufficient for a top-tier AI venue. The main evaluation uses only 60 MusicNet segments, lacks subjective listening tests, has no statistical uncertainty, and provides only limited quantitative comparison to baselines.

Several central claims are not supported. The abstract and conclusion claim evaluation up to 500 ms and mention MTG, but the presented results only show MusicNet gaps up to 300 ms. Claims of state-of-the-art or superior performance are therefore overstated.

The method description omits important implementation details needed for reproducibility and technical assessment, including model size, number of layers/heads, diffusion schedule, number of sampling steps, conditioning mechanism, masking procedure, whether known tokens are clamped during reverse diffusion, and tokenizer configuration.

The novelty is moderate. Discrete diffusion over tokenized audio is a natural extension of existing discrete diffusion and audio-tokenizer work; the paper does not provide enough analysis to show why this formulation is technically new beyond applying known machinery to audio inpainting.

The baseline treatment is weak. The paper appears to compare partly against values from prior work rather than a fully controlled reimplementation, does not include strong recent long-gap models such as MAID or GAN-based long inpainting in the main quantitative table, and does not provide enough detail to assess fairness of preprocessing, sample rate, gap placement, or metric computation.

There are no ablations isolating the effect of the discrete diffusion model, WavTokenizer, crossfade, context conditioning, token length, training data size, or gap duration distribution, making it hard to understand what actually drives the reported gains.

The paper lacks perceptual validation despite being an audio-quality task. Objective metrics such as FAD and LSD are useful but not sufficient to establish musical coherence or listener preference for inpainted segments.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard: the title repeatedly misspells 'inpainting', there are numerous grammatical errors, the audio example link is missing, figure labels contain typos, and some equations/notations are introduced without clear connection to the implemented model.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and practical problem: audio inpainting for music, especially for gaps beyond the very short durations handled by many classical methods.

The core idea of performing inpainting in a discrete audio-token space using a pretrained tokenizer is plausible and potentially interesting, and it connects recent discrete diffusion work with audio restoration.
The manuscript includes comparisons against several relevant prior methods from the audio inpainting literature and evaluates with multiple objective metrics, including FAD, LSD, and ODG.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is far too weak for the strength of the claims. The paper claims competitive or superior performance and even robustness to 500 ms gaps, but the main reported table only covers the proposed method up to 300 ms, and the claimed 500 ms MTG evaluation is not actually presented in the results.

Baselines are inadequately reported. Figure 3 visually compares against prior methods, but there is no numerical table, no statistical uncertainty, no implementation details, and no clear evidence that baselines were rerun under identical conditions rather than borrowed from prior work. This makes the central superiority claim hard to trust.

The evaluation is narrow: only 60 MusicNet segments are used, there is no subjective listening study, no MOS or preference test, and no analysis of perceptual artifacts at boundaries or musical coherence, which are crucial for audio inpainting.

There are no ablations isolating the contribution of the discrete diffusion model, WavTokenizer, token masking strategy, crossfade, model size, number of diffusion steps, or comparison to simpler masked-token prediction/transformer baselines. As a result, the paper does not establish why the proposed design is necessary.

The technical description is incomplete for reproducibility. Important architectural and training details are missing, including transformer depth/width, codebook size used, masking/noise schedule, conditioning mechanism, sampling procedure, number of reverse steps, gap-to-token alignment, inference hyperparameters, and evaluation preprocessing.

The novelty is overstated. Discrete diffusion over tokenized audio and masked discrete modeling are already established in adjacent audio generation settings, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish its contribution beyond applying these ingredients to inpainting.

Some claims appear unsupported or inconsistent. The abstract mentions MTG and 500 ms gaps, while the experiments primarily describe MusicNet and only show up to 300 ms. The conclusion again claims strong 500 ms performance without presenting the corresponding data.

The writing and presentation are below the standard expected at a top-tier AI venue, with repeated typos such as “Inpanting,” awkward phrasing, unclear equations/notation, and captions/claims that are not backed by complete quantitative evidence.

The method may inherit tokenizer reconstruction errors and quantization artifacts, but the paper does not evaluate the tokenizer upper bound, oracle token reconstruction, or whether metric gains come from the codec/crossfade rather than the diffusion model.

Overall, while the direction is reasonable, the paper currently reads more like a preliminary experiment than a mature top-tier conference submission: the core claims are not adequately supported, reproducibility is limited, and the experimental validation is incomplete.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and timely idea: applying discrete diffusion over WavTokenizer audio tokens for music inpainting, which is a plausible and potentially useful alternative to waveform or spectrogram diffusion.

The method is conceptually simple and well motivated: tokenization reduces sequence length and may help model longer-range musical structure while preserving unmasked waveform regions at inference time.
The experiments report encouraging trends on MusicNet, especially for longer gaps, with FAD/LSD/ODG results suggesting competitive performance against CQT-Diff+ and classical baselines.
The paper is mostly easy to follow at a high level and connects the approach to relevant audio inpainting, diffusion, and discrete diffusion literature.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not yet convincing for a top-tier AI venue. The main quantitative table reports only the proposed method, while baseline comparisons appear only in a figure without exact numbers, uncertainty estimates, or details on whether baselines were rerun under identical conditions.

Several strong claims are insufficiently supported. The abstract and conclusion mention MTG and 500 ms gaps, but the paper does not present MTG results or a 500 ms table/analysis in the visible experimental section.

Important implementation details are missing, including DiT depth/width, number of parameters, diffusion schedule, number of sampling steps, masking strategy, conditioning mechanism, and how known tokens are enforced during reverse diffusion. This limits reproducibility.

There are no ablations isolating the contribution of discrete diffusion, WavTokenizer, crossfading, token replacement, model size, or training data scale. A tokenizer reconstruction upper bound would also be important.

The experimental scope is narrow: only 60 MusicNet test segments are evaluated, with no subjective listening study despite the perceptual nature of the task. FAD on such a small evaluation set may be unstable.
The paper’s positioning overstates novelty somewhat, since discrete diffusion on audio tokens has prior precedent in audio generation, even if not directly for inpainting.

Writing and presentation need polish. There are many typos and grammatical issues, including the title spelling “Inpanting,” missing audio-example URL, formatting errors in equations/references, and unclear figure/table captions.
The method is promising, but the current evidence falls slightly short of acceptance because the empirical comparison and reproducibility details are incomplete.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical audio restoration problem, especially medium-to-long music gaps where classical and continuous-domain methods often degrade.

The main idea of performing inpainting in a compressed discrete audio-token space is sensible and potentially useful; combining WavTokenizer with discrete diffusion is a natural way to reduce sequence complexity while preserving higher-level musical structure.
The experiments cover two relevant music datasets, MusicNet and MAESTRO, and compare against several appropriate prior inpainting baselines, including CQT-Diff+ and GAN-based methods.
The reported results are promising: AIDD improves over CQT-Diff+ on MusicNet for 200-300 ms gaps on FAD/LSD and achieves strong ODG scores on MAESTRO, including the 750 ms setting.

The paper includes an ablation over span masking and derivative regularization, which helps support the claim that the proposed training modifications contribute beyond the base discrete diffusion objective.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The method largely combines an existing audio tokenizer, an existing discrete diffusion objective, and a DiT backbone; the two proposed training modifications are plausible but not deeply analyzed theoretically or empirically.

Several methodological details are underspecified: the exact DiT architecture, conditioning mechanism, mask handling at inference, token-gap alignment, number of reverse diffusion steps, tokenizer configuration, and how the derivative loss is computed from a categorical score model are not sufficiently clear for confident reproduction.

The derivative-based regularization is not fully justified. Smoothness in learned codebook embedding space does not necessarily correspond to perceptual or musical smoothness, and the paper does not analyze whether neighboring token embeddings have meaningful temporal geometry.

The evaluation is too limited for strong audio-quality claims. There are no human listening tests, no MOS/preference study, and no qualitative or failure-case analysis, despite the perceptual nature of music inpainting.

The MusicNet evaluation uses only 60 test segments and gaps up to 300 ms, while the stronger long-gap claim relies mainly on MAESTRO ODG results. The evidence for robust long-gap inpainting is therefore thinner than the abstract and conclusion suggest.

The MAESTRO setup is insufficiently reproducible: the training subset is randomly selected and only promised upon request, and the exact test subset size and sampling protocol are not clearly reported.

Baseline comparability is uncertain. It is unclear whether all baselines were rerun under identical preprocessing and evaluation code, or whether some values were taken from prior work. The use of different metrics across datasets further weakens direct claims of state-of-the-art performance.

The reporting suggests possible cherry-picking: Table 1 states that the AIDD result is the highest reported score, and the ablation uses unequal training budgets, with the base model trained for 400k steps but variants trained for 100k steps.
Statistical support is weak. Some ODG/LSD entries include standard deviations, but FAD generally does not; no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided for the main comparisons.
Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code is said to be released only upon acceptance, the audio example link is missing, and important hyperparameters beyond a small table are absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful audio restoration problem and proposes a sensible high-level direction: performing inpainting in a discrete audio-token space rather than directly over waveform or time-frequency representations.

Using a pretrained WavTokenizer with a discrete diffusion transformer is a plausible architecture for improving long-gap coherence, and the paper gives an understandable overview of the intended pipeline.
The experiments cover two music datasets and include comparisons to several classical, GAN-based, and diffusion-based baselines, with some reported improvements on objective metrics.
The paper includes an ablation table for span masking and derivative-based regularization, which is a useful attempt to isolate the proposed training components.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not convincing enough for a top-tier venue. The MAESTRO comparison uses only ODG, while MusicNet uses FAD/LSD/ODG; the subset of MAESTRO is unspecified; and it is unclear whether baselines were rerun under the same preprocessing, masking, tokenizer, train/test split, and evaluation implementation.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper claims consistent superiority and state-of-the-art performance, but Table 1 shows CQT-Diff+ has better FAD at 150 ms, Table 3 does not show the combined method consistently best, and many differences are very small or within reported variability.

The ablation study is weak. Reported gains from derivative regularization and span masking are marginal, sometimes inconsistent, and not supported by significance testing. The derivative loss appears especially under-justified because smoothness in learned token embedding space does not necessarily correspond to perceptual audio smoothness.

Important methodological details are missing or unclear: how silence gaps are converted to diffusion masks after tokenization, how conditioning on observed context is enforced during reverse diffusion, model size and architecture details, tokenizer configuration, sequence lengths, number of diffusion steps, and exact noise schedules.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper says code will be released only after acceptance, the audio demo link is blank, the MAESTRO subset will be provided only on request, and the supplementary hyperparameter table is too sparse to reproduce the experiments.

The comparison to prior work is potentially unfair. Some baselines target different datasets, gap lengths, or evaluation protocols, and the paper does not establish that the reported numbers are directly comparable. The claim that the model uses less data and compute than prior work is not substantiated with controlled experiments.

The paper lacks perceptual listening tests, which are particularly important for audio inpainting because objective metrics such as FAD, LSD, and ODG may not fully capture musical coherence or boundary artifacts.

Technical presentation has gaps and inconsistencies. The derivative-based loss is described over predicted embeddings, but the main model is trained to estimate discrete diffusion score ratios; the connection between these outputs is not specified clearly. The span-based absorbing process is also not fully reconciled with the DWDSE formulation.

The writing contains several imprecise or unpolished statements, including vague novelty claims, repeated claims of robustness without sufficient support, and future-work claims about language models that are not motivated by the experiments.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and timely direction: performing audio inpainting via discrete diffusion over WavTokenizer tokens rather than continuous waveform or spectrogram representations. This is a sensible formulation that could improve semantic coherence for longer gaps.
The method is conceptually simple and well motivated, combining a pretrained audio tokenizer, a DiT-style discrete diffusion model, span-based masking, and derivative-based regularization.

The empirical results are encouraging: AIDD improves over several classical, GAN-based, and diffusion baselines on MusicNet for 200-300 ms gaps, and shows strong ODG results on MAESTRO at 375 ms and 750 ms.
The paper includes useful ablations over span masking and derivative regularization, which provide some evidence that the proposed training modifications help over the base DWDSE model.
The computational claims are attractive: the method appears to achieve competitive results with a relatively modest single-GPU training setup.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not yet fully convincing for a top-tier AI venue. MusicNet evaluation uses only 60 test segments, and MAESTRO details are underspecified, including the exact subset size and selection procedure.

The comparison protocol is unclear. It is not always evident whether baselines were re-run under identical preprocessing, gap placement, sample rates, and evaluation code, or whether numbers were taken from prior work. This matters because audio metrics are sensitive to implementation details.

The paper relies entirely on objective metrics, with no human listening study. For music inpainting, perceptual quality and musical coherence are central, and FAD/LSD/ODG alone are insufficient to fully support the strongest claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details are missing or vague, including model size, architecture hyperparameters, tokenizer configuration/checkpoint, noise schedule, number of reverse diffusion steps, sampling procedure, exact MAESTRO subset, and baseline implementations. The code/audio examples are promised but not actually available in the manuscript.

Some claims are overstated. The paper claims state-of-the-art performance and robust long-gap inpainting, but MusicNet results only go to 300 ms, MAESTRO reports only ODG, and the 750 ms improvement over bin2bin-MIDI is very small relative to the reported variance.

The ablation interpretation is too strong. The combined method is not consistently best across all metrics; for example, derivative-only variants sometimes obtain better FAD or comparable ODG. The incremental value of combining span masking and derivative loss is therefore not clearly established.

The novelty is positive but somewhat incremental: the work mainly combines a pretrained audio tokenizer, an existing discrete diffusion objective, and standard transformer machinery. The new losses/masking are plausible but not deeply analyzed theoretically or empirically.

Presentation has several polish issues, including missing audio-example link text, formatting problems in tables, grammatical errors, and some imprecise statements that make the paper feel less mature than a top-tier submission.
